A fighter loyal to Yemen's government on the front line around Mount al-Midan in Taiz province, on 26 October 2026 (Ahmad al-Basha/AFP)

It wasn’t easy for Mukhtar, 45, to flee his home in the village where he was born and raised, 50 kilometres south of Taiz city. However, he felt forced to leave in 2019, believing that the Houthis (also known as Ansar Allah) were fighting for a noble cause in Yemen and that he needed to support them.
Mukhtar had been living in an area controlled by the Saudi Arabia-backed government, and the prospect of staying there any longer had become dangerous. Many of his relatives, including his brothers and cousins, supported government forces, and he feared he might be detained, like so many others.
“Many Ansar Allah supporters were detained or fled their villages; not just fighters, but civilians and sheikhs who supported them. So there was no choice but to flee my village and live in Ansar Allah-controlled areas,” Mukhtar told Middle East Eye.
Back in his village, Mukhtar had worked as a farmer and part-time land broker, but he lost his livelihood when he fled. When he reached a Houthi area, he joined the group, convinced that they were driven not by money but by a desire to defend Islam.
“Ansar Allah’s project is for the hereafter; they implement what is in the Quran rather than following the orders of foreign countries. Theirs is a project for the afterworld, not a project of mercenaries,” Mukhtar added.
On 3 September, Houthi forces launched a heavy offensive against government troops in southern Hodeidah and the western district of Taiz, seizing large areas of both governorates.

data.author: Oscar Rickett

Trump says he will 'see what happens' with Iran after 1 January
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that Washington would "see what happens" as regards its war on Iran after 1 January.
“We're going to have a new year coming up, and we'll see what happens after January 1. But they've been nasty,” Trump told Fox News during his trip to China.
Trump made the comments during an interview in which he was asked about a CNN report that Iran was planning to detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington. A dirty bomb uses conventional explosives to spread radioactive material.
Trump downplayed such a threat, saying “I don't think so”, when asked if people in the capital should be alarmed.

data.title: Middle East Eye: China issues 'peace declaration' agreed with Trump and Putin
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
China issues 'peace declaration' agreed with Trump and Putin
China has released a “peace declaration” it said its President Xi Jinping and his US and Russian counterparts Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin had agreed on at their unprecedented three-way meeting, where they said nuclear wars were futile and should never be fought.
All three countries committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security, according to a four-point declaration published by Chinese official media Xinhua.
The leaders reportedly discussed Russia's war in Ukraine and the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, Xinhua said.
The three heads of state also agreed on reform for a "more effective" United Nations, and said that the International Criminal Court and similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction, according to the declaration.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Critics accuse The New York Times of promoting Iran war propaganda
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
Critics accuse The New York Times of promoting Iran war propaganda
The New York Times (NYT) is facing widespread criticism over its report claiming that some of Iran's water infrastructure may have been built to support its missile programme, with critics accusing the newspaper of promoting war propaganda and providing a justification for attacks on Iranian civilian infrastructure.
Published on Monday with the headline "War May Answer Longtime Riddle of Iranian Dams Built for No Clear Reason", the article examines the geographical overlap between dam and water infrastructure projects and sites recently struck during the US-Israeli war on Iran. It suggests that some of these projects may have been designed, at least in part, to support military facilities.
One of the two journalists who wrote the piece, Sanam Mahoozi, shared the article on X, writing: “Why has Iran kept building dams amid a severe water crisis? @ErikaSolomon and I examined a striking overlap between water projects and military sites. Could some have served a dual purpose? No conclusive evidence, but questions worth exploring.”
The Iranian Water Diplomacy Association noted on Tuesday "with serious concern" the discrepancies in the report, including the fact that geographical proximity between struck sites and water infrastructure sites does not establish military use.
Read more: Critics accuse The New York Times of promoting Iran war propaganda

data.title: Middle East Eye: Iraq strikes 'compromise' deal with Iran-backed Kataeb Hezbollah
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
Iraq strikes 'compromise' deal with Iran-backed Kataeb Hezbollah
Iraq has reached a compromise with Kataeb Hezbollah, the Iran-backed paramilitary group, three senior security officials told Reuters, after Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi readied security forces to move against the group.
Iraqi officials had accused the Iraq-based group of running a smuggling ring that siphoned off hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of state-owned oil.
Under the deal brokered by senior Shia political leaders to avert what could have been a civil war, government forces were expected to move into Kataeb Hezbollah stronghold of Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday, according to three security officials familiar with the deal.
Kataeb forces would move to other areas, Lieutenant General Saad Maan, head of Iraq's Security Media Cell, told Reuters.
Reflecting the gravity of the situation, Iraqi Shia political sources said Esmail Qaani, commander of Iran's elite Revolutionary Guards' Quds Force, arrived in Baghdad late on Monday to help defuse tensions with Kataeb Hezbollah, Tehran's most powerful militia ally in Iraq.
A spokesperson for Kataeb Hezbollah said the group's secretary-general, Abu Hussein al-Hamidawi, met Qaani, Hadi al-Amiri, head of the Badr Organization, another influential Iran-aligned militia, and other influential figures in a bid to prevent an escalation.
Participants described the outcome of the talks as positive in a statement issued on Thursday.

data.title: Middle East Eye: How British sanctions are already having a material impact in the West Bank
data.author: Fleur Hargreaves
data.summary:
How British sanctions are already having a material impact in the West Bank
British sanctions targeting illegal Israeli settlements already appear to be having a material impact, even though most of the planned measures have yet to come into force.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced the first set of sanctions on Tuesday. They targeted eight Israeli construction, property development and architectural businesses.
One of those firms is Har Hevron Development Company, which the British government said "carries out construction and infrastructure works for, and supplies housing units to, Israeli settlements and outposts in the southern West Bank".
On Thursday, Eliram Azulai, head of the Har Hevron Regional Council, told Israeli media that its foreign trade accounts have already been frozen by two banks.
Azulai added that "this is only spreading further", saying he had heard other companies have had their services blocked.

Officials had accused Kataeb Hezbollah of running a smuggling ring from Jurf al-Sakhar that siphoned off hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of state-owned oil.

Lieutenant General Saad Maan, head of Iraq's Security Media Cell, said the armed group's forces would move to other areas.

It will be led by Lieutenant General Ahmed Hatem Hamid, alongside deputy commanders Major General Hussein Ali Nassif for defence affairs, and Adi Abdel-Imam Mussah for the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF).
The deal was brokered by senior Shia political leaders, with Esmail Qaani, commander of Iran's elite Quds Force, also arriving in Baghdad late on Monday to help defuse the situation.

data.title: Middle East Eye: US builds up forces around Iran, but can it sustain another war?
data.author: Fleur Hargreaves
data.summary:
US builds up forces around Iran, but can it sustain another war?
A third US aircraft carrier and its escorts arrived in the Middle East on Sunday, further bolstering Washington's military presence around Iran.
The deployment of the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group comes even as the US maintains it has no intention of resuming large-scale combat operations and will continue seeking to pressure Iran through a blockade.
“We don’t need to conduct military strikes if we’re achieving the same objective through economic means and economic pressure,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on 10 November.
The US military build-up suggests however that the economic blockade Washington has enforced against Iran since 14 July is unlikely to push Tehran into capitulation any time soon. Attacks in the Gulf in recent days have highlighted Iran's capacity to respond to perceived US threats and its willingness to do so.
Meanwhile, media reports suggest that the US Navy is approaching breaking point, with sailors facing shortages of fresh food.

Judge Navi Pillay enters the International Court of Justice in The Hague, the Netherlands, to deliver its judgment against Myanmar, on 19 November 2026 (Reuters/Piroschka van de Wouw)
Off
The International Court of Justice's landmark ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya could have far-reaching consequences for Israel, after judges rejected the argument that military operations against armed groups provided an adequate explanation for a campaign of mass killings, sexual violence and widespread destruction.
The judgment, the first time the UN's highest court has found a state responsible for genocide, offers South Africa a potentially significant legal precedent in its case accusing Israel of committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, particularly over how judges assess genocidal intent when a state claims its military actions are driven by security objectives.
In a 9-6 decision on Thursday, the ICJ found that Myanmar's security forces had committed genocide against the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State during the military's 2017 operations.
"The only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the protected group, namely the Rohingya population in Northern Rakhine State," the court said.
The judgment is particularly significant for South Africa's case, which hinges on establishing that Israel acted with the specific intention of destroying Palestinians, in whole or in part, as a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.

The UK's trade envoy to Israel has endorsed a social media account which has disparagingly labelled the foreign secretary the "Palestine secretary" and repeatedly attacked the Labour government, claiming it is trying to appease Muslims.
Earlier this week Byline Times reported that @habibi_uk, the anonymous account on X which campaigns against pro-Palestine public figures in the UK, is the American-British grandson of the philosopher Bertrand Russell and a US State Department-trained expert in "political-military diplomacy" called Benjamin Tait.
Tait has previously worked with Lord Ian Austin, a former Labour MP and life peer who has been the trade envoy to Israel under successive governments since July 2019.
Austin posted on X on Wednesday, in response to the Habibi account: "Keep going", followed by two emojis of a muscled arm and two clapping emojis.

Reports suggest that investigation likely centres on US activist Fergie Chambers' extradition case
Former Palestine Action activist Bridget Shergalis (Supplied)
Off
Two former Palestine Action activists in the US are risking imprisonment by refusing to testify before a federal grand jury in New Hampshire on Wednesday.
Sophie Ross and Bridget Shergalis risk up to 18 months in prison for contempt of court for defying grand jury subpoenas issued by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).
The FBI has not disclosed any details of the investigation, nor named a defendant.
Reports suggest that it is likely that the target of the investigation is Fergie Chambers, a millionaire left-wing donor currently facing extradition to the US from Spain, where he is detained pending a decision by a Spanish court.
The extradition order is in part based on allegations that Chambers helped fund a protest in November 2023 targeting Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems in Merrimack, New Hampshire.
Ross and Shergalis also participated in the action and were sentenced to 60 days in prison for misdemeanour convictions.
Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Shergalis referred to Israel's actions in Gaza when she described the pair’s refusal to testify as “an effort to not incriminate ourselves or anyone who believes it is their moral obligation to stop genocide”.

– Sophie Ross, former Palestine Action activist

There are many levers western governments can pull to halt the moral and legal abomination that is Israel's genocide in Gaza. They just choose not to
A Palestinian woman walks along a road as residents are forced to evacuate by another Israeli attack on tent shelters in Nuseirat, central Gaza Strip, on 18 November 2026 (AFP)
Off
The Genocide Convention, drafted in 1948 and inspired by the work of a Polish-Jewish lawyer who escaped the Holocaust, could not be clearer.
Among its provisions, it defines the crime of genocide as “deliberately inflicting on [a national, ethnic, racial or religious] group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part”.
“Deliberately” indicates that there must be intent.
For months, the United Nations and international aid agencies have warned that Israel is blocking aid supplies into Gaza, further endangering the survival of some two million Palestinians already living in the bleakest of conditions.
Israel’s three-year bombing campaign has already engineered, for those who have survived it, their utter destitution and dependency on handouts from the international community.
This week Israel was forced to make public its own aid figures and they resoundingly corroborate those warnings.
Since Israel agreed a ceasefire in Gaza just over a year ago, it has broken its commitment - month after month - to allow humanitarian supplies into the enclave.
A freedom of information request from the Haaretz newspaper shows that, since March, the aid trucks entering the enclave have never gotten close to the number Israel agreed was required to address the population’s basic needs.
Critical shortages
According to the ceasefire’s terms, Israel was supposed to allow in 18,200 trucks a month, or 600 a day.
Last March, Israel let in only a quarter of that number: 4,779.
